wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache and Mourvèdre in roughly equal leading parts, with Syrah and Counoise next and smaller parts of the other permitted varieties: the estate grows all thirteen.
wine.sites: One large block around the château at Courthézon, on the northern edge of the appellation and open to the Mistral: rolled stones over sand, clay and limestone, planted to all thirteen varieties, with much old Mourvèdre.
wine.making: Each variety is picked by hand and fermented apart, Mourvèdre and Syrah in conical wooden vats and the others in concrete and steel. The grapes are destemmed and, by long habit of the estate, heated briefly and cooled again before about two weeks of maceration. The blend is then raised for about a year in large old oak foudres and bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Kirsch and blackberry over leather, game and dried thyme, with black olive, liquorice and a note of truffle as it ages; firm and savoury rather than sweet, the Mourvèdre giving grip and a long, meaty finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it often closes between about five and ten years, then opens again and keeps for two or three decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The popes' new castle: the cru between Orange and Avignon that permits thirteen named varieties.
The estate at Courthézon, on the northern edge of the appellation.

records.table: All thirteen permitted varieties grow at Château de Beaucastel, and its Châteauneuf-du-Pape carries far more Mourvèdre than most. Savoury rather than sweet, leather, game and kirsch, it can close up in its middle years, so decant it and be patient.
records.story: Courthézon, on the northern edge of Châteauneuf, has known the name Beaucastel since 1549, when, by the estate's account, a man of that name bought a barn and land at Coudoulet. In 1909 the property was bought by a forebear of the Perrin family, who rebuilt its vineyard; it passed to his son-in-law, the first Perrin there, who enlarged it, and then to that son-in-law's son, Jacques Perrin, who ran it until his death in 1978. By the estate's account Jacques Perrin was a forerunner of organic farming from the 1960s, and he brought back Mourvèdre, a variety that had almost vanished from the appellation; it gives the wine its savoury frame of leather and game. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, decreed in 1936 among the first appellations of France, allows thirteen varieties, and Beaucastel grows every one of them. In 1989 his sons first made Hommage à Jacques Perrin, a Mourvèdre led selection kept for strong years, and that same year the family and their American importer bought land at Paso Robles in California, the start of Tablas Creek. Mourvèdre belongs in any talk of Châteauneuf because of Beaucastel, the counterweight to Grenache alone.

others.name: Hommage à Jacques Perrin
others.note: A Mourvèdre led selection built on the estate's oldest Mourvèdre, first made in 1989 and only in strong vintages.

others.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Roussanne Vieilles Vignes
others.note: The white of old Roussanne vines, a Châteauneuf blanc with a long life.

others.name: Coudoulet de Beaucastel
others.note: Côtes du Rhône from vines just outside the appellation, across the road from the estate.

traps: Coudoulet de Beaucastel is Côtes du Rhône, not Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
Thirteen varieties by name, eighteen when the colour forms of Grenache, Clairette and Piquepoul are counted apart.
Hommage à Jacques Perrin is Mourvèdre led and not made every year; the estate's Châteauneuf is the annual wine.

cards.front: Château de Beaucastel: how many of Châteauneuf's permitted varieties does it grow, and which one sets it apart?
cards.back: All thirteen; an unusually large share of Mourvèdre.

cards.front: What does Château de Beaucastel do to its harvest before fermentation?
cards.back: It heats the destemmed grapes briefly, then cools them again, before they macerate and ferment.

questions.q: A guest finds Château de Beaucastel's Châteauneuf-du-Pape more savoury and gamey than the one before it. Which grape do you credit?
opts: Mourvèdre
Cinsault
Grenache Blanc

questions.exp: Beaucastel grows far more Mourvèdre than most of the appellation, and it gives leather, game and grip; Cinsault is light and perfumed, and Grenache Blanc and Clairette are white.

questions.q: In 1989 the family of Château de Beaucastel first made a Mourvèdre led selection. Whom does its name honour?
opts: Jacques Perrin, who ran the estate until 1978
The leader of the growers' union of 1923
The popes of Avignon, builders of the castle
Claude Chappe, inventor of the telegraph
questions.exp: Hommage à Jacques Perrin honours the man who ran Beaucastel until his death in 1978 and brought back its Mourvèdre; the growers' union of 1923 was led by Baron Le Roy.

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.sites: Parcels of sand with some clay, ringed by woods north east of the village, most of them facing north, so the Grenache ripens slowly in shade and cool air; none of the rolled stones of La Crau.
wine.making: Grenache from old vines, cropped at very low yields, is fermented and then raised in old foudres and demi-muids, none of them new and some of them decades old, before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Kirsch, raspberry and wild strawberry over incense, rose petal and dried orange peel; pale in the glass, silky and light on its feet for its strength, with fine tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Charming within a few years in a ripe vintage, it grows more savoury over fifteen to twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant gently if at all, so as to keep the perfume; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's name; on a French label château names a wine estate, whatever its buildings.
The cru between Orange and Avignon, which allows a blend of varieties yet does not require one.

records.table: Pale enough to surprise a guest, Château Rayas's Châteauneuf-du-Pape is Grenache alone, grown on cool, north facing sand among the woods rather than on the famous stones. Kirsch, incense and rose, it drinks more like a red Burgundy than a southern blend, so pour it into a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Rayas lies among woods north east of the village of Châteauneuf, on sand rather than stone. It was founded in 1880 by a notary of the Reynaud family who had lost his hearing and turned to the vine. His son, who had studied agriculture, bottled the estate's first wine in 1920 and printed Premier Grand Cru on its labels, a rank of his own making that exasperated the local authorities, since Châteauneuf has no official classification. He added Château des Tours at Sarrians in the 1930s and Château de Fonsalette in the Côtes du Rhône in 1945. On his death in 1978 one of his sons took charge of Rayas and Fonsalette, until his own sudden death, without children, in 1997. A nephew who had been running Château des Tours then took Rayas on, keeping its Grenache alone, its very low yields and its old wood until his death in 2025. The appellation allows thirteen varieties, yet Rayas showed that a Châteauneuf could be pale, perfumed and of one grape, and that cool sand could matter as much as the rolled stones. Colour and weight, it teaches, are not the measure of a southern red.

others.name: Pignan
others.note: A named parcel of the same estate, bottled apart as a second Châteauneuf, not a separate property.

others.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc

others.name: Château de Fonsalette
others.note: The family's Côtes du Rhône estate, bought in 1945 and made under the same hand.

Pignan is a Rayas cuvée, not a separate estate; Fonsalette is Côtes du Rhône, not Châteauneuf.
The Premier Grand Cru the founder's son printed on Rayas labels was his own wording, not a rank: Châteauneuf has no official classification.

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape La Crau
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, about two thirds, with Mourvèdre and Syrah in near equal smaller parts and a little Cinsault, Clairette and other permitted varieties.
wine.sites: The plateau of La Crau in the south east of the appellation near Bédarrides, at about 130 metres: rolled Alpine pebbles, the galets roulés, over Miocene molasse and a thick bed of stony clay that holds water through the summer.
wine.making: Picked by hand and sorted three times, at the vine and in the cellar. The grapes are destemmed, in some years with a share of whole bunches kept, and fermented in vat; the blend is then raised for fifteen to sixteen months in large French oak foudres of thirty to sixty hectolitres and bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Kirsch and blackberry over dried thyme, lavender and warm stone, with leather and liquorice from the Mourvèdre; full and firm rather than sweet, with fine, dusty tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous for a few years after release, it then closes for a while and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The stony plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape where the vines grow, not the Crau plain of Provence.
The old telegraph: the optical signal tower that once stood on the plateau.

records.table: On the stony plateau of La Crau, where rolled stones store the day's heat, Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe grows its Châteauneuf-du-Pape La Crau. Grenache led, with Mourvèdre and Syrah, it tastes of kirsch, thyme and warm stone, and ages for twenty years.
records.story: The domaine is named for a tower. Claude Chappe (1763 to 1805) devised the optical telegraph, a chain of towers with movable arms that passed messages across France from hilltop to hilltop, and its first line opened in 1794. By the domaine's account a tower of his system was raised in 1821 on La Crau, the stony plateau south east of the village. In 1891, the year the family dates its work from, the Bruniers began to plant vines on the plateau, among stones so thick that the soil beneath them can barely be seen, and a later generation gave the estate the old tower's name. When the appellation was decreed in 1936 the plateau lay within it. The galets roulés, pebbles carried down from the Alps by the ancient Rhône, store the day's heat and give it back at night, while the clay beneath holds water through the summer, so the old Grenache ripens fully without drying out. The family made La Crau its flagship, with Télégramme, from younger vines, beside it as a second wine. Ask what the stones of Châteauneuf actually do, and Vieux Télégraphe is the glass that answers.

others.name: Télégramme
others.note: The second wine, Châteauneuf-du-Pape from the domaine's younger vines.

others.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc
others.note: The white of Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc and Roussanne from the same domaine.

traps: The name comes from an optical telegraph tower on the plateau, not from a vineyard.
La Crau here is a plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, not the Crau plain of Provence.
Télégramme is the second wine, from younger vines, not a lighter style of La Crau.

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, the larger part, with an unusually high share of Mourvèdre, from a fifth to nearly a third, some Syrah and small parts of other permitted varieties.
wine.sites: Around two dozen parcels scattered across the appellation's varied soils, blended so that no single soil leads; among them the old vine plot beside the ruins of the popes' castle that gave the estate its name.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed and fermented in vat; the wine is raised in vat and in large old oak foudres, never new, before the blend is bottled at the domaine, and no special cuvée is drawn off.
wine.glass: Raspberry, kirsch and black cherry over dried thyme, lavender and liquorice, with a savoury edge of leather from the Mourvèdre; fresh and structured for Châteauneuf, with firm, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Fruity on release, it closes after a few years and opens again towards its tenth year, keeping for two decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's name, from one old vine plot by the popes' castle; the wine blends many parcels.
The cru named for the castle the popes of Avignon built above the village in the fourteenth century.

records.table: One red a year and no special cuvée above it: Clos des Papes blends its Châteauneuf-du-Pape from parcels all over the appellation, with more Mourvèdre than most. Fresh and firm, raspberry, thyme and leather, it opens again towards its tenth year.
records.story: Records of the Avril family in Châteauneuf go back, as the family tells it, to 1600, in a village named for the castle the popes of Avignon built above it between 1317 and 1333. In 1896 an Avril first bottled the estate's wine under the name Clos des Papes, taken from an old vine plot beside the ruins of that castle. In 1923 the growers of the village formed a union under Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié (1890 to 1967) to win strict rules on where their wine grew, from which grapes and at what ripeness, and on 15 May 1936 Châteauneuf-du-Pape became one of the first appellations of France. The family's holding grew to around two dozen parcels in every corner of the appellation. Where other houses set their old vines apart in prestige cuvées, Clos des Papes kept to one red and one white, and its red carries more Mourvèdre than most. That refusal to divide is the estate's signature. On a list it stands for the whole appellation in one bottle, and its white, from six varieties, deserves a place beside it.

others.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc
others.note: The white, from six varieties in roughly equal parts, a wine that ages for years.

The estate makes one red and no prestige cuvée, so there is no grander Clos des Papes to trade up to.
Mourvèdre matters more here than in most Châteauneuf, which leans on Grenache.

questions.q: Clos des Papes stands in the village whose growers formed a union in 1923. In which year did Châteauneuf-du-Pape become an appellation?
questions.exp: The decree of 15 May 1936 made law of what the growers' union of 1923 had fought for; 1909 is the year Beaucastel was bought, and 1971 the year Gigondas became a cru.

The name settled: Decanter and Skurnik give it from an old vine plot beside the ruins of the popes' castle, so the library's trap that no clos of that name exists now reads as no single clos; Skurnik calls the plot walled and Decanter does not, so the record says a plot.

Confirmed: the family since 1600 by its own site, the first bottling of 1896 under the name, the union of 1923 under Baron Le Roy, his dates and his chair of the INAO, the decree of 15 May 1936, the castle of 1317 to 1333, about two dozen parcels and full destemming in three accounts against one.

Taken out: each variety fermented apart and a year or more in foudre, since Decanter has only a third of the red in foudre for a year and nothing settles the rest; the village selling in bulk in 1896; Mourvèdre for freshness and structure.
Nobody of the family is named: accounts confuse the grower of 1896 with his descendants, the father of recent decades died in 2009 with no birth year read, and the son is living.

changed: wine.grapes: Mourvèdre from a fifth to nearly a third, by the blends of several vintages.

wine.sites: the appellation's varied soils, where it said rolled stones, sand and limestone, for want of a source on each parcel; the old vine plot by the castle ruins that gave the name, by Decanter and Skurnik.

wine.making: destemmed by three accounts against one, raised in vat and in old foudres never new, by Decanter, the Wine Scholar Guild and a merchant, where it said each variety fermented apart and a year or more in foudres.
wine.label: the name from one old vine plot by the popes' castle, where it said no single walled vineyard; the castle dated to the fourteenth century.

story: the family from 1600 by its own site; the castle built between 1317 and 1333, by the appellation's page and Wikipedia; the name from the plot by the ruins; the union of 1923 under Baron Le Roy and the decree of 15 May 1936, by the appellation's page and INAO; where it said the seventeenth century, rules drawn up in 1923, the village selling in bulk in 1896, parcels added through the twentieth century and Mourvèdre for freshness and structure.

cards[1]: the union of 1923 and the Baron's chair of the INAO from 1947, by the Château Fortia page and wein-plus, where it said rules that fed into appellation law.
questions[0]: the third option is now a bottling of the plot by the castle, and the explanation says that plot goes into the one red, where it said no walled clos existed.

open: Whether the plot by the castle is walled: Skurnik says so, Decanter does not; the record says a plot.
Destemming: three accounts say in full, one since 1991, and one aggregator says whole bunches; the record says destemmed.
How much of the red goes to foudre, a third for a year by Decanter or the whole by others, is left unsaid.

wine.name: Gigondas
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, about seven tenths, with Mourvèdre and Syrah in near equal smaller parts and a touch of Cinsault.
wine.sites: The estate's bush vines around Gigondas below the limestone crags of the Dentelles de Montmirail, on limestone soils in one of the cooler corners of the cru, where cool nights keep the wine fresh.
wine.making: Fermented as whole bunches on native yeasts; the wine is then raised for about a year, part in concrete vats and part in barrels, a small share of them new and the rest used for a few wines, and bottled at the estate without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Black cherry and blackberry over smoke, dried thyme and black pepper, with a cool, stony freshness from the limestone; firm but fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage, it is at its fullest between five and fifteen years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour when young; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A cru under the Dentelles, red and rosé since 1971 and white too from the 2023 vintage.
The family estate's own wine; the house's merchant range, from bought grapes, is labelled Saint Cosme alone.

records.table: At the foot of the Dentelles, limestone and cool nights keep Château de Saint Cosme's Gigondas fresh: Grenache led, with Mourvèdre and Syrah, fermented as whole bunches. Black cherry, smoke and pepper, it is a firmer, cooler neighbour to Châteauneuf, made for game or lamb.
records.story: Under the jagged limestone of the Dentelles de Montmirail, Saint Cosme stands on ground worked since Roman times: vats cut into the limestone beneath the château are held to be Gallo-Roman. The Barruol family has been there since 1490 by most accounts, with 1570 in others. Gigondas, long a commune of the Côtes du Rhône Villages, became on 6 January 1971 the first of them raised to a cru of its own, for red and rosé. In 1992 a son of the family took charge after his father fell ill, and later in that decade, by the family's account, set up a merchant business beside the estate for wines from bought grapes, labelled Saint Cosme alone. Beside its Gigondas the estate bottles lieux-dits apart, Le Claux, Hominis Fides and Le Poste, and an old vine Valbelle. From the 2023 vintage the appellation added white wine to its red and rosé. The estate's Gigondas, whole bunches of Grenache with Mourvèdre and Syrah from its own vines, introduces the house and shows that Gigondas is not simply a Châteauneuf from the next valley.

traps: Gigondas has been a cru since 1971; before that it was a commune of the Côtes du Rhône Villages.
The Saint Cosme merchant wines are made from bought grapes; Château de Saint Cosme is the estate.
Gigondas is mostly Grenache, like Châteauneuf, but its limestone and height give a cooler, firmer wine.

questions.q: A guest wants a southern Rhône red fresher and firmer than Châteauneuf. Why might Château de Saint Cosme's Gigondas suit?
opts: Limestone and cool nights under the Dentelles
Rolled stones that store the summer heat
Sea breezes off the Mediterranean coast
A large share of white grapes in the blend
questions.exp: Gigondas sits high under the limestone Dentelles, and cooler nights keep it fresh; rolled stones that hold the heat are the mark of La Crau in Châteauneuf.

questions.q: Château de Saint Cosme's village was promoted from Côtes du Rhône Villages to a cru of its own. In which year?
questions.exp: Gigondas became a cru on 6 January 1971, the first of the Villages; 1936 was the decree of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and 2023 the first vintage of white Gigondas.

report: Rechecked with six searches on 12 November 2026; Inter Rhône and INAO settle the cru of 6 January 1971 and the white from 2023, and the importer's sheets of two vintages, Grape Collective and a merchant settle the making.

Changed: the whole crop is fermented as whole bunches on native yeasts, not the Syrah alone, and raised about a year in concrete and in barrels with a small share new, bottled unfined and unfiltered; Mourvèdre stands level with Syrah, not a little.
The family since 1490 by most accounts (iDealwine, the importer), with 1570 reported from the estate's own home page; the library's 1570 is reported as in tension and the record gives both.

Taken out: the chapel of Saint Cosme as the source of the name (one account places the chapel by Le Poste and no more), the lower yields and tighter boundary of 1971, and Valbelle as a lieu-dit; Vacqueyras's year left out of an explanation for want of a source read.
The merchant business is dated 1997 in a Decanter interview whose address names a living person, so the record says later in that decade, by the family's account.
The pick is kept: the estate's own Gigondas carries the château's name and is the wine the house pours most widely; Valbelle, the library's flagship, was found in vintages to 2015 only.

changed: wine.grapes: about seven tenths Grenache, Mourvèdre and Syrah near equal and a touch of Cinsault, by the importer's sheets and a merchant, where it said Syrah much of it whole bunch and a little Mourvèdre.
wine.sites: bush vines on limestone in one of the cooler corners of the cru, by the importer's sheet and Inter Rhône, where it said clay and limestone and height.

wine.making: the whole crop as whole bunches on native yeasts, about a year in concrete and in barrels with a small share new, no fining or filtration, by the importer's sheets, Grape Collective and a merchant, where it said the Syrah largely whole bunch and vats, large casks and older barrels.
table: Grenache led with Mourvèdre and Syrah, all fermented as whole bunches.

story: 1490 by most accounts with 1570 in others, where it said since 1570; the chapel naming the estate cut; the cru of 6 January 1971 as the first of the Villages, from Inter Rhône; the son of 1992 and the merchant business later in that decade, by Wine Spectator and the family's interview, where it said a new generation in the 1990s; Valbelle no longer a lieu-dit; the lower yields and tighter boundary of 1971 cut.

others: Valbelle the old vine selection, Le Claux on yellowish limestone marl and Hominis Fides on Miocene sand and clay, by the importer, where they said a long standing selection above the Gigondas, clay and limestone and lighter.
